text: Univariate analysis means one variable at a time. Before you compare columns to each other, you need to know what each column looks like on its own. We keep using the made-up customer table from the last lesson.

For each numeric column, look for four things. The center: what is a typical value? The spread: how much do values vary? The shape: is it symmetric, skewed, or lumpy? And oddities: any gaps, spikes, or extreme values? Numbers answer some of this, but a histogram answers all four at once.

Here are three histograms side by side, one for age, one for tenure in months, and one for total spend. A short loop calls seaborn's histplot on each column with thirty bins. Bins matter, so try a few values rather than trusting one.

Age is roughly bell shaped. Tenure has a long right tail: most customers are fairly new, and a few have stayed for years. Total spend is the strange one. Almost everything is crammed into a single bar near zero, and two dots sit far to the right. The chart is telling you something is extreme.

The skew method puts a number on the shape. Near zero means symmetric. Age is about zero point one eight. Tenure and orders lean right, and total spend is fifteen, dramatically skewed by those two huge values. With right skew, the median is usually a better typical value than the mean. Here the median spend is about one twenty-four, the mean about one eighty-eight.

For categories, count them. North has one hundred fifty customers, East one forty-four, West one hundred seven, South ninety-nine. Pass normalize equals true to see proportions instead. Watch for rare categories, dominant ones, and spelling variants, which value counts exposes immediately.
Center, spread, shape, oddities. Next up, bivariate analysis: comparing two variables at a time.
